newsitem.title: TAIWAN: BASEBALL-WOMEN'S TEAM WIN OVER FANS.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-WOMEN'S TEAM WIN OVER FANS.

text.p: Imagine playing baseball overseas with the entire local crowd roaring for your side.
They cheer when you strike out one of their guys, In fact, they cheer every time you throw a strike.

When the opposing pitcher brushes your player back, they boo and hiss as if he had tried to hit Cal Ripken in Baltimore. And if you hit a home run, they erupt into the kind of frenzy normally reserved for World Series triumphs.
It happens. If your team is all women. If your team is the Colorado Silver Bullets.
The Silver Bullets were invited by the Taiwan Major League for a six-game series to promote the league, which starts early next year alongside the seven-year-old Chinese professional league.

And in a recent 15-2 loss to a fledging Taiwan professional side, they were cheered to the echo by a passionate crowd of 2,000. "It was great hearing a foreign crowd cheer us on like that, to know they appreciate what we're doing, " outfielder Tammy Holmes said lofting a two-run homer over the left-field wall.
"That's why we're out here, to provide a little entertainment for the people, " said Silver Bullet's acting manager Bruce Crabbe.
The Silver Bullets, formed three years ago, arrived here after a season during which they played 52 games against semi-professional men's team across the United States, winning 18.
And they provided a perfect warm-up act in the Taiwan Major League's drive for fan support, opponents who generate newspaper headlines but pose no threat on the field.

"The unique thing is we play against men only," said Crabbe. "We do get in over our heads and we admit it. Right now we're doing it to promote the Taiwan Major League and to promote women's baseball internationally."
The novelty of women on the diamond has provided a refreshing break to a game marred this year by gambling and game-fixing allegations involving players and coaches from the old league.
Charges that teams threw games for payments from gamblers and gangsters are being investigated by the justice ministry.
"The women can really play," said Cheng Wei-teh as he watched the Bullets lose a second contest 11-3 in a more respectable showing.
"All the skills are there, except they have a bit less power."
Amateur softballer Tsai Min-li added: "Their hustle and genuine enthusiasm are something I want to have in my own game."
The praise may have been a little generous as the Silver Bullets managed only four hits and made several miscues which were not tagged as errors by a generous scorekeeper.
"It helps when you get your butt kicked and everyone is still like "Oh great job'," Holmes quipped.
Still, Holmes's homer was a morale booster and starting pitcher Pam Davis threw some quality pitches.
Former American league player Sam Horn was certainly impressed. Horn was nearly struck out by Davis in his only at-bat and drew a walk only after fouling some tough pitches.
"Before the game you definitely tell yourself you don't want to get beat by women," Horn said. "But when I had two strikes on me all I could think about was how not to strike out.
"The women are showing good heart by coming out here, even if the level of competition was a little too tough."
